name: Argument from Fallacy
description: A claim gets dismissed just because one argument for it was flawed, as if a bad argument automatically proves the conclusion false. That is a reasoning mistake about arguments, not strong evidence of a distinct named cognitive-bias effect.
design_relevance_note: Occasionally relevant in strategy reviews, experiment debates, policy critique, and AI-safety arguments: a sound idea can be rejected because one advocate defended it badly. But this is much more a logic/argumentation concept than a design-psychology one.
myth_risk_note: This entry's existing no_rigorous_backing_found status is confirmed. Argument from fallacy ('the fallacy fallacy' -- inferring a claim is false because the argument given for it is fallacious) is a logic/philosophy construct, not an empirically-tested cognitive bias. This pass's search returned papers on other, distinct fallacies (the gambler's fallacy fallacy, the Cartesian fallacy fallacy, the conjunction fallacy in children) and unrelated methodology/AI-evaluation papers, but no peer-reviewed empirical study measuring 'argument from fallacy' as a psychological bias in human reasoning.
prevalence_note: Mostly a critical-thinking or logic-classroom term; it appears only occasionally in design or product conversation, usually inside broader reasoning critiques rather than as a standard UX concept.
